newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia-EU warfare on rural trade said over.
newsitem.headline: Australia-EU warfare on rural trade said over.

text.p: Australia and Europe had emerged from trench warfare on traded agricultural products, Aneurin Rhys Hughes, the European Union's (EU) Ambassador to Australia and New Zealand, said on Thursday.

EU reforms on agricultural subsidies in an international context were on-going, with the EU policy to remove all production subsidies in the next few years, he told the New South Wales Farmers Association general council meeting.
The EU market was not fully open, but neither were markets fully open in the U.S., the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation group or in Australia, he said.
"We in the EU would come into some difficulty if we were to try to get cereals or sugar or dairy produce, chicken meat or even salmon into Australia," he said.

On EU export refunds, Hughes said that the EU had to bring its export prices into line with "international trading reality". "Unlike the U.S. we are concerned with domestic self-sufficiency, not export market share," he said.
The effect of EU subsidies on world grain market prices was small compared with production and weather, he said.
EU wheat refunds had been reduced to US$5.00-$7.00 a tonne then were suspended on April 21 because of potential record drought in parts of the EU and frost in Kansas, he said.
The EU was moving to reduce agricultural support levels to as close to the world price level as politically possible, he said.
It was moving to direct subsidy payments to farmers as compensation for loss of income with price reductions.
It was also moving toward removal of all production subsidies and further liberalisation of the world agricultural market, he said.
"(But) we will do it at our own pace and at a rate which is socially and politically sustainable," he said.
Responding to questions, Hughes said agricultural intervention by the EU would continue, not on full production but through direct subsidisation of farmers' income.

Asked if the EU would return to subsidisation of export grain in the forseeable future, Hughes said the EU Commission proposal was that by the turn of the decade all production subsidies would have been removed.
Export refunds were already fairly irrelevant, he said.

Arguing that the EU was not ultra-protectionist against imports and that its exports were not produced at dumped prices, Hughes said the EU was the largest importer of agricultural products in the world with a recent annual growth rate of 10 percent.
It took A$2 billion worth iof Australian agricultural products last year, he said.
The EU had had a trade deficit in agricultural products for the past four years while the U.S. had had an agricultural trade surplus in the same period.
Enlargement of the EU, with membership negotiations beginning this year with four countries from east and central Europe, provided a further "strong whip on our backs for ... change", he said.

However, questions put to Hughes by NSW Farmers Association delegates were so sharply critical of the EU's record on agricultural subsidies they suggested the ambassador's view of an end to trench warfare may be not fully shared.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
